Apple devices have always been known for having the highest-quality LCD screens in the industry, and this remains true for today's MacBook. The company has successively improved image quality through Retina displays and mini-LED backlighting technology. This is also why Apple has not been in a rush to adopt OLED technology.

However, Apple is indeed gradually transitioning to OLED. The company first applied this display technology to the Apple Watch, then expanded it to iPhone and iPad models, and the MacBook Pro is the next batch of upgrades...

Further down the line, the MacBook Air and iMac are also expected to switch from IPS LCD to OLED.

Nearly every related report we publish—including yesterday's piece on the Mac roadmap—draws one to several comments worrying about OLED burn-in, so it's worth exploring the causes and whether this remains an issue on today's higher-spec displays.

What is OLED burn-in?

LCD screen pixels do not emit light on their own; instead, they are illuminated by a set of LED backlights. Take Apple's mini-LED screens as an example—the greater number of backlight LEDs allows for more precise control of brightness in specific areas of the screen.

OLED screens are an entirely different technology. Each pixel emits its own light, resulting in more vivid colours and deeper blacks, while unused pixels can be switched off completely. As the name suggests, the chemical components are organic—that is, they contain carbon-based molecules rather than silicon-based molecules—which makes them more prone to uneven degradation.

In addition, each pixel also receives considerably more power. Over time, pixels gradually age, and because some pixels are used more frequently, they age faster, leading to uneven wear.

When the same image is displayed continuously for extended periods—such as a station logo on a TV screen—the relevant pixels age faster and lose brightness compared with other areas. The OLED panel will attempt to compensate by outputting more power to the weaker pixels, but this actually accelerates the ageing process further, eventually leaving a permanent ghost image of that repeated content on the screen.

Do we need to worry about burn-in on MacBooks?

The short answer is almost no, for four reasons.

First, usage patterns. Burn-in most commonly occurs when a display shows static content for prolonged periods, such as airport flight information screens and CCTV footage. The likelihood of burn-in on a laptop is much lower, because even static content like menu bar icons and the Mac dock is regularly covered by full-screen applications.

Second, modern OLED panels are overall more durable, with a significantly lower chance of pixel burn-in. Our iPhone home screen icons sometimes remain unchanged for years, yet no one has ever complained about burn-in issues.

Third, burn-in is most likely to occur when a display operates at maximum brightness for extended periods. This is extremely rare on laptop screens, especially as technology advances and maximum brightness is already quite dazzling.

Finally, Apple will adopt tandem OLED panels. This design stacks two layers together, with each layer requiring only about half the power to achieve the same brightness, substantially reducing the energy stress that causes pixel ageing.

Taking all these factors together, even if you plan to keep your next Mac longer than usual, the chances of seeing burn-in on an OLED MacBook Pro are extremely low.
